procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated February 4, 1966 of the Punjab High Court in Criminal Revision No. 34-M of 1965, quashing the proceedings pending against the respondent.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent filed a petition under s. 561A of the Cr.P.C. in the High Court for quashing the proceedings pending against him. The High Court of Punjab quashed the proceedings pending against the respondent, mainly on the ground that until the First Information Report which had been registered at the instance of the respondent had been cancelled by the Magistrates it was not open to the police to ask for prosecution of the respondent for the alleged offences. The High Court also referred to the complaint which had been filed by the respondent on the same allegations on which the First Information Report had been registered and which was still pending.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the Judgment of the High Court of Punjab.

directions: The proceedings in respect of offences other than those under ss. 182, 211 and 193 shall continue.
The proceedings in relation to offences under ss. 182, 211 and 193 alleged to have been committed by the respondent shall stand quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution of the respondent for offences under ss. 182, 193 and 211 of the Indian Penal Code could be proceeded with.

facts: The respondent filed a First Information Report (FIR) with the police.

After investigation, the police concluded the respondent's allegations were false and filed a charge-sheet against him for several offences, including under sections 182, 193, and 211 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
Meanwhile, the respondent filed a private complaint before a Magistrate based on the same facts as his original FIR.
This private complaint was pending and was considered a "proceeding in any Court".
law: Section 195(1)(b) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) bars a court from taking cognizance of certain offences, including those under sections 193 and 211 of the IPC, when they are alleged to have been committed in, or in relation to, any proceeding in any court.
Prosecution for such offences can only be initiated on a written complaint by that specific court, not on a police report.
application: The Court found that the respondent's pending private complaint before the Magistrate constituted a "proceeding in any Court."

Since the police charge-sheet for offences under ss. 193 and 211 was based on the same facts as the respondent's pending complaint, these alleged offences were considered to be committed "in relation to" that court proceeding.
Therefore, the bar under s. 195(1)(b) of the Cr.P.C. applied, preventing the Magistrate from taking cognizance of these offences based on the police report.

Regarding the offence under s. 182, the Court reasoned that the facts also disclosed the more serious offence under s. 211. To allow the police to proceed under s. 182 would effectively circumvent the specific legal bar for prosecuting the s. 211 offence, which arose from the same allegations.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the prosecution of the respondent for offences under sections 182, 193, and 211 of the IPC could not be proceeded with. The existence of the respondent's own pending complaint in a Magistrate's court triggered the statutory bar in Section 195(1)(b) of the Cr.P.C., which requires that prosecution for such offences, when related to a court proceeding, must be initiated by a complaint from that court itself, not by a police charge-sheet.

issue.issue_text: Whether the proceedings for other offences (such as under ss. 467, 471, 385 IPC), which were part of the same charge sheet, can be continued even if the proceedings for offences under ss. 182, 193 and 211 are quashed.

facts: A single police charge sheet was filed against the respondent for multiple offences, including those under ss. 182, 193, and 211 IPC, as well as other offences like ss. 467, 471, and 385 IPC.
The High Court had quashed the entire proceedings, including those for the other offences.
law: The Court cited the well-settled legal principle that when police are investigating a cognizable offence, they are not barred from also investigating any non-cognizable offence that arises from the same set of facts.
Police can legally include such non-cognizable offences in the same charge sheet they present for a cognizable offence.
application: The Court applied this principle to the case, noting that the quashing of proceedings for the offences under ss. 182, 193, and 211 (which had specific procedural requirements for taking cognizance) did not affect the validity of the investigation into the other offences like ss. 467, 471, and 385.

Since the police were empowered to investigate these other offences alongside the main cognizable offence and include them in the charge sheet, there was no legal reason to stop the proceedings for them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there was no objection to the continuance of the proceedings for the offences other than those under ss. 182, 211, and 193. Therefore, it allowed the appeal in part, ruling that the prosecution for offences like ss. 467, 471, and 385 could continue, even though the proceedings for the other specific offences were quashed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution of the respondent for offences under ss. 182, 193 and 211 of the Indian Penal Code could be proceeded with.
appellant_arguments: The State (appellant) argued that there was no legal requirement for the First Information Report (FIR) filed by the respondent to be formally cancelled by a Magistrate before the police could submit a charge sheet against the respondent for offences committed by him as the informant.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the prosecution could not proceed because his own complaint, based on the same allegations as the FIR, was still pending in court. Therefore, any alleged offence under s. 211 or s. 193 IPC was committed in relation to that court proceeding, and cognizance could only be taken upon a complaint by that court, as required by s. 195(1)(b) of the Cr.P.C. Allowing the police to prosecute directly would circumvent this mandatory legal procedure.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the proceedings for other offences (such as under ss. 467, 471, 385 IPC), which were part of the same charge sheet, can be continued even if the proceedings for offences under ss. 182, 193 and 211 are quashed.
appellant_arguments: The procedural bar under s. 195 of the Cr.P.C. applies only to the specific offences mentioned therein (ss. 182, 193, 211) and does not affect the validity of the entire charge sheet. Therefore, the prosecution for other distinct offences should be allowed to continue.
respondent_arguments: The respondent sought to have the entire proceedings quashed, implying that the invalidity of the charges under ss. 182, 193, and 211 tainted the entire prosecution.

cases.case_name: M. L. Sethi v. R. P. Kapur
cases.principle: When a complaint filed by an informant is being proceeded with, based on the same facts as a First Information Report, a Magistrate cannot take cognizance of an offence under s. 211 of the Penal Code unless there has been proper compliance with the provisions of s. 195(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A Magistrate is barred from taking cognizance of an offence under ss. 193 and 211 of the Indian Penal Code if that offence is alleged to have been committed in, or in relation to, any proceeding in any court. However, while investigating the commission of a cognizable offence, a police officer is not debarred from investigating any non-cognizable offence which may arise out of the same facts.
obiter: It is not considered proper or necessary for the court to go into points which were not agitated before the High Court.
It will be open to a party to raise points not covered by the judgment before the appropriate courts below.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Once a complaint filed by an informant is being proceeded with in court, which is based on the same facts and allegations as a First Information Report they had previously registered, it is not open to a Magistrate to take cognizance of offences like ss. 193 or 211 IPC against that informant based on a police report. Cognizance for such offences can only be taken if there has been proper compliance with the provisions of s. 195(1)(b) of the Cr.P.C., which requires a complaint from the court where the proceedings are pending.
legal_tests_applied: Whether any proceeding in any Court existed when the Magistrate took cognizance of the offence. If a proceeding existed and the offence (e.g., under s. 211 I.P.C.) was alleged to have been committed in or in relation to such a proceeding, the Magistrate would be barred from taking cognizance by s. 195(1)(b) of the Cr.P.C. unless there is a complaint by that Court.

The bar under s. 195 Cr.P.C. applies only to the specific offences mentioned therein and does not debar the prosecution for other distinct offences, even if they arise from the same facts and are part of the same charge sheet.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant (State) lost on the issue of prosecuting for offences under ss. 193 and 211 IPC because the respondent's own complaint, based on the same allegations as his FIR, was already pending in court. This pending complaint constituted a 'proceeding in any Court'.

Because a court proceeding existed, the alleged offences of making a false charge (s. 211) and giving false evidence (s. 193) were considered to be 'in relation to' that proceeding, thereby triggering the mandatory procedural bar of s. 195(1)(b) Cr.P.C.
The police could not circumvent the requirement of s. 195(1)(b) Cr.P.C. (which necessitates a complaint from the court itself) by filing their own charge sheet for these specific offences.
why_respondent_won: The respondent succeeded in having the proceedings under ss. 182, 193, and 211 IPC quashed because his own complaint on the same facts was pending before a Magistrate. This meant the alleged offences were committed 'in relation to' a court proceeding.

The existence of the respondent's pending complaint invoked the procedural safeguard of s. 195(1)(b) Cr.P.C., which prohibits a court from taking cognizance of offences like ss. 193 and 211 except on the complaint in writing of the court where the offence was committed or in relation to which it was committed.
The court accepted that allowing the police to prosecute directly would defeat or circumvent the provisions of s. 195(1)(b) Cr.P.C.
policy_considerations: Allowing a police prosecution for an offence under s. 211 IPC while the informant's own complaint is pending would lead to anomalous results. For example, if the informant's complaint is ultimately dismissed and that Magistrate refuses to lodge a complaint under s. 195(1)(b), the provisions of that section would be defeated or circumvented if the police could independently move the Magistrate to take cognizance on a police report.
